newsitem.title: USA: TransTexas Gas's Stanley plans next great escape.
newsitem.headline: TransTexas Gas's Stanley plans next great escape.

text.p: Like the famous escape artist, Harry Houdini, oil and gas mogul John Stanley is attempting to free himself from a financial straightjacket.
Stanley's companies, TransAmerican Refining Corp and TransTexas Gas Corp, are bound by agreements with holders of approximately $1.24 billion in outstanding junk bonds.
The bondholder covenants, the financial equivalent of locks and chains, have put Stanley in a dangerous position.

TransAmerican Refining, which is wholly owned by Stanley, could be in technical default on its debt if it fails to complete the first phase of modernization of an oil refinery in Good Hope, Louisiana by July 15. The original date for completion of phase one had been February 15, but bondholders have agreed to extend the deadline until mid-July.

Market sources said TransAmerican, which has been working on the modernization for several years, needs to raise around $100 million to finish phase one and at least $200 million to complete the second phase.
A TransAmerican spokesman declined to comment. Stanley himself could not be reached for comment.
To complete the project, Stanley would like to use cash generated from TransTexas Gas, a profitable oil and gas exploration company in which he controls roughly an 80 percent stake.
However, Stanley is prevented from doing so by other bondholder covenants, analysts said.

To escape from these restraints, Stanley plans to replace the outstanding junk bonds via a $1.53 billion new debt offering by parent company TransAmerican Energy Corp (see list below). TransAmerican Energy is the parent company of both TransAmerican Refining and TransTexas Gas.

Jefferies & Co Inc, a Los Angeles-based investment bank specializing in the energy industry, will be the sole underwriter of the mega, private placement offering, which is expected to price next week, TransAmerican Energy said.
The bonds will presumably have less restrictive covenants, allowing Stanley to shift money between its various subsidiaries, analysts said.
Additionally, experts said the new debt was likely to be significantly less expensive than the outstanding bonds, some of which carry interest rates as high as 18.5 percent.

To complete the refinancing, Stanley plans to raise another $1.1 billion by selling a unit of TransTexas Gas to a consortium of leasing and financial companies managed by GATX Capital Corp, a leasing company. The unit owns the lucrative Lobo Trend natural gas reserves in southern Texas.
Some of the proceeds from the transactions will be used to buy back up to $371 million of outstanding TransTexas stock held by Stanley-controlled entities and public stockholders.
TransAmerican said the size of Stanley's stake in TransTexas is not expected to be affected by the refinancing.

"The biggest risk here is that the (Lobo Trend) sale doesn't go through," said Ronald Habackus, a high-yield energy analyst at Merrill Lynch & Co Inc. "If it doesn't go through, it's unlikely (Stanley) can complete the refinery and then things get messy."
Stanley, however, is not a stranger to audacious and risky escapes. His companies have filed for bankruptcy on two occasions but he managed to maintain control of the oil and gas empire.
Investors certainly will question whether Stanley's latest financial feat will be authentic or simply smoke and mirrors.

Analysts pointed out that following the transactions, TransAmerican Energy will be more leveraged with almost $400 million in additional debt. "Every time he refinances, he has come out with a bigger issue," noted one analyst.

Buyers of the new bonds will place bets that Stanley is able to complete the Good Hope refinery and operate it profitably. Analysts said refining is a commoditized business, subject to chronic overcapacity in the recent past.

But others said Stanley's strategy could pay off. "We have seen a lot of consolidation in the refinery business. More consolidation usually leads to decreased competition and raises the price of refinery products," said T. Michael Hoye, energy analyst at KDP Investment Advisors Inc of Montpelier, Vermont.
Experts noted the new offering also was likely to benefit from the current strength of the junk bond market.

"The timing of this deal is perfect. We are experiencing one of the hottest new issue markets (in junk bonds) and there is a lot of demand for bonds in the oil and gas industry, which has strong fundamentals," said Erik Dybesland, energy junk bond analyst with Bear Stearns & Co Inc.

Finally, despite his past difficulties with creditors, analysts noted that Stanley has scored points with bondholders in recent deals. They pointed out that Stanley has promised to give investors who tender their outstanding bonds an instant premium of at least 10 percent. Many current bondholders are expected to be investors in the new securities.

"He has shown that he was able to generate enough value in TransTexas (the exploration and production company) to make sure everyone is satisfied with their original investment," said Merrill's Habackus.
-- PROPOSED NEW HIGH-YIELD BOND OFFERING --
*TRANSAMERICAN ENERGY CORP $425 million senior secured notes due 2002
*TRANSAMERICAN ENERGY CORP $1.105 million (principal amount) senior secured discount notes due 2002
-- OUTSTANDING HIGH-YIELD BONDS TO BE TENDERED --
*TRANSTEXAS GAS CORP $800 million 11.5 percent senior secured notes due 2002 at 111.5 percent of principal amount.
*TRANAMERICAN REFINING CORP $340 million 18.5 percent guaranteed first mortgage discount notes due 2002 at 110 percent of principal amount of accrued and unpaid interest
*TRANSAMERICAN REFINING CORP $100 million 16.5 percent guaranteed first mortgage notes due 2003 at 110 percent of principal amount of accrued and unpaid interest
